questions.question: How do you write a FizzBuzz program in Java?
questions.title: FizzBuzz Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Print 'Fizz' for multiples of 3, 'Buzz' for multiples of 5, 'FizzBuzz' for both, and the number otherwise.** Check the combined case first. This tests basic loops, conditionals, and the modulo operator — and more importantly, your attention to the order of checks.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic programming ability, correct order of conditions, and clean code style
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Checking n%3==0 and n%5==0 separately before checking the combined case — prints 'Fizz' instead of 'FizzBuzz' for 15
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note that you check FizzBuzz first and explain why, or offer the string concatenation variant

sections.title: Order of Conditions Matters
sections.content: The critical rule: check `n % 15 == 0` (or `n % 3 == 0 && n % 5 == 0`) **first**, then separately 3 and 5. If you check 3 first, multiples of 15 print 'Fizz' only. Classic form: `for (int i = 1; i <= 100; i++) { if (i%15==0) print 'FizzBuzz'; else if (i%3==0) print 'Fizz'; else if (i%5==0) print 'Buzz'; else print i; }`

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Check divisible by both (15 or &&) FIRST
- Then divisible by 3, then by 5, then number
- Modulo operator %: n % 3 == 0 means n is divisible by 3
- Clean alternative: build string by concatenating 'Fizz' and 'Buzz'
- String concatenation version is more extensible for more rules
- Loop: for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)
- This is a gatekeeping question — get it right quickly

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: FizzBuzz is straightforward but has one gotcha: you must check for divisibility by both three and five first. If you check three first, a number like fifteen would print Fizz instead of FizzBuzz. My approach: loop from one to one hundred, check if divisible by fifteen for FizzBuzz, then by three for Fizz, then by five for Buzz, otherwise print the number. I'd also mention the string concatenation variant where you build an empty string, append Fizz if divisible by three, append Buzz if divisible by five, and print the number if the string is still empty — this scales better if you add more rules.

questions.question: How do you check if a number is prime in Java?
questions.title: Prime Number Check Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **A number is prime if it has no divisors other than 1 and itself.** Check divisors from 2 to √n — if any divide n evenly, it's not prime. O(√n) time. Edge cases: numbers ≤ 1 are not prime; 2 is the only even prime.

interviewer_intent.testing: Mathematical reasoning and ability to optimize — the sqrt(n) optimization is the expected answer
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Checking up to n instead of sqrt(n), giving O(n) when O(sqrt(n)) is trivially achievable
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why sqrt(n) is sufficient: if n = a*b and a > sqrt(n), then b < sqrt(n) — you'd already have found b

sections.title: Check up to Square Root
sections.content: **Why sqrt(n)?** If n has a factor greater than √n, its corresponding pair factor must be less than √n — and we'd already have found it. Algorithm: handle edge cases (n ≤ 1: false; n == 2: true; n even: false). Then check odd divisors from 3 to √n with `i += 2` (skip evens — already handled). If any `n % i == 0` — not prime. O(√n) time, O(1) space.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Edge cases first: ≤1 not prime, 2 is prime, even > 2 not prime
- Loop: i from 3 to sqrt(n), step by 2 (only check odd divisors)
- Termination: i*i <= n (equivalent to i <= sqrt(n), avoids floating point)
- i*i <= n vs Math.sqrt: avoid floating point precision issues
- O(√n) time — critical optimization from O(n)
- Sieve of Eratosthenes: O(n log log n) for all primes up to n

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I check divisors from 2 up to the square root of n. The key insight is that if n has a factor larger than its square root, the corresponding co-factor must be smaller than the square root — so we'd already encounter it. I handle edge cases first: return false for anything less than or equal to 1, return true for 2, return false for any even number greater than 2. Then I check odd numbers from 3 up to sqrt(n), using the condition i times i less than or equal to n to avoid floating point. This is O(sqrt(n)) time. If the interviewer asks about finding all primes up to n, I'd describe the Sieve of Eratosthenes.

questions.question: How do you find the second largest element in an array?
questions.title: Second Largest Element Array Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Single pass with two variables: largest and secondLargest.** When `arr[i] > largest`: secondLargest = largest, largest = arr[i]. When `arr[i] < largest && arr[i] > secondLargest`: secondLargest = arr[i]. O(n) time, O(1) space — no sorting needed.

interviewer_intent.testing: In-place single-pass thinking — can you avoid sorting O(n log n) for a simpler O(n) solution
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Sorting the array first — O(n log n) — when a single O(n) pass suffices
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Handle edge cases: array length < 2, all elements equal (no second largest), duplicates

sections.title: Single Pass, Two Variables
sections.content: Initialize `largest = Integer.MIN_VALUE`, `secondLargest = Integer.MIN_VALUE`. For each element: if `arr[i] > largest` — update `secondLargest = largest`, then `largest = arr[i]`. Else if `arr[i] > secondLargest && arr[i] != largest` — update `secondLargest = arr[i]`. The `!= largest` condition handles duplicates. If `secondLargest == Integer.MIN_VALUE` after the loop — no second largest exists.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Two variables: largest and secondLargest
- Update secondLargest before overwriting largest
- Handle duplicates: arr[i] != largest condition
- Edge: array length < 2 → no second largest
- Edge: all same elements → no second largest
- Time: O(n), Space: O(1)
- Avoid sorting: O(n) beats O(n log n)
- Can extend to k-th largest with a PriorityQueue

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I use two variables: largest and secondLargest, both initialized to the minimum integer value. In a single pass: if the current element is greater than largest, I first copy largest into secondLargest, then update largest. If the current element is not the new largest but is greater than secondLargest and different from largest, I update secondLargest. The duplicate check is important — otherwise an array like [5, 5, 3] would incorrectly give 5 as the second largest. This is O(n) time and O(1) space. For the k-th largest element in general, I'd use a min-heap of size k.

questions.question: How do you rotate an array by k positions in Java?
questions.title: Rotate Array Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Reverse the entire array, reverse the first k elements, reverse the remaining n-k elements.** This achieves right rotation by k in O(n) time and O(1) space. Normalize k with `k = k % n` to handle k > n.

interviewer_intent.testing: In-place array manipulation — whether you know the three-reversal trick vs naive approach
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using an extra array O(n) space or doing k separate single-step rotations O(n*k)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why the three-reversal trick works with a small example, and handle the k > n edge case

sections.title: Three-Reversal Trick
sections.content: To right-rotate [1,2,3,4,5] by 2: result should be [4,5,1,2,3]. Steps: (1) Reverse all → [5,4,3,2,1]. (2) Reverse first 2 → [4,5,3,2,1]. (3) Reverse remaining 3 → [4,5,1,2,3]. **Done.** Normalize: `k = k % n` (if k=7 and n=5, that's same as k=2). O(n) time, O(1) space. The reverse operation is O(n) and done 3 times.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Normalize: k = k % n (handles k > n and k == 0)
- Step 1: reverse entire array
- Step 2: reverse first k elements
- Step 3: reverse last n-k elements
- Time: O(n), Space: O(1)
- Alternative: extra array — copy [n-k..n-1] then [0..n-k-1] — O(n) space
- Left rotation by k = right rotation by n-k
- Write a helper reverse(arr, start, end) for clean code

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The elegant O(1) space solution is the three-reversal technique. First I normalize k to k modulo n to handle k greater than n. Then I reverse the entire array, reverse the first k elements, and reverse the remaining n minus k elements. Let me trace through: rotating [1,2,3,4,5] right by 2 — reverse all gives [5,4,3,2,1], reverse first 2 gives [4,5,3,2,1], reverse last 3 gives [4,5,1,2,3] — which is the correct right rotation. I write a helper reverse method taking start and end indices to keep the code clean. This is O(n) time and O(1) space.

questions.question: How do you find the second largest element in an array in a single pass?
questions.title: Second Largest Element in an Array: Single-Pass O(n) Solution
questions.direct_answer: Track two variables — largest and secondLargest — updating them in one pass: when a new element beats largest, demote largest to secondLargest before updating largest; when it beats only secondLargest, update secondLargest directly.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can solve a classic problem in O(n) with O(1) space rather than sorting
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using Integer.MIN_VALUE as the initial value but forgetting to handle the edge case where all elements are equal (secondLargest stays MIN_VALUE)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Handle edge cases explicitly: all identical elements, array with fewer than two elements, and negative numbers

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
I maintain two variables initialised to Integer.MIN_VALUE: largest and secondLargest. I iterate through the array once.

For each element, I check: if it is strictly greater than largest, I set secondLargest equal to largest and then set largest equal to the current element. This is the demotion step — the old largest becomes the new second largest. If the element is not greater than largest but is strictly greater than secondLargest and not equal to largest, I update secondLargest to the current element.

The 'not equal to largest' condition is important for handling duplicates — if the array contains [5, 5, 3], the second largest should be 3, not 5 again.

After the loop, if secondLargest is still Integer.MIN_VALUE, it means all elements were identical or the array had fewer than two distinct values — I return an indication that no second largest exists.

This solution is O(n) time and O(1) space. Sorting would give O(n log n) time and O(1) or O(n) space depending on the sort algorithm. The interviewer typically wants the single-pass solution and will probe edge cases, so I address them proactively.

sections.title: Key Points
content: If element > largest: secondLargest = largest; largest = element
Else if element > secondLargest AND element != largest: secondLargest = element
The != largest guard handles duplicate maximum values correctly
O(n) time, O(1) space; handle edge case where no second distinct element exists

questions.question: How do you check if a number is prime efficiently?
questions.title: Efficient Prime Number Check: O(√n) Algorithm
questions.direct_answer: Check divisors only up to the square root of n — if n has a factor larger than √n, it must also have a corresponding factor smaller than √n, so checking beyond √n is unnecessary.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the O(√n) optimisation and can explain the mathematical reasoning behind it
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing the O(n) loop checking all divisors up to n-1 without knowing the √n optimisation exists
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the mathematical justification, handle all edge cases (n<=1, n=2, even numbers), and mention the Sieve of Eratosthenes for checking primality of many numbers

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
I start with the edge cases. If n is less than or equal to 1 it is not prime — this covers 0, 1, and negatives. If n equals 2 it is prime — 2 is the smallest and only even prime. If n is even and greater than 2, it is not prime — I return false immediately.

For odd numbers from 3 upward I check potential divisors only up to the square root of n. The condition I use is `i * i <= n` to avoid calling Math.sqrt, which involves floating-point arithmetic and can introduce precision issues. I increment by 2 to skip even divisors since I already handled even numbers above. If any divisor evenly divides n I return false. If the loop completes without finding a divisor I return true.

The mathematical reason is: if n equals a times b, and both a and b are greater than √n, then a times b would be greater than n — a contradiction. So at least one factor must be less than or equal to √n. This means if we find no divisor up to √n, there is no divisor at all.

Time complexity is O(√n) versus O(n) for the naive approach. For a single number this is usually sufficient in an interview. If the interviewer asks about checking many numbers I mention the Sieve of Eratosthenes, which finds all primes up to N in O(N log log N) time.

content: Edge cases first: n <= 1 → false; n == 2 → true; n even and > 2 → false
Loop: `for (int i = 3; i * i <= n; i += 2)` — checks only odd divisors up to √n
Use `i * i <= n` not `i <= Math.sqrt(n)` to avoid floating-point precision issues
O(√n) time vs O(n) naive — explain the mathematical justification
For many primes: mention Sieve of Eratosthenes O(N log log N)
